units.title: How Web Pages Work
units.tip: A web page is written in HTML, which gives structure and content. Tags wrap content to give it meaning. Elements are tags plus their content. Attributes add extra information to tags.

exercises.question: What does HTML stand for?
exercises.answer: HyperText Markup Language
exercises.explain: HTML is the standard language for creating web pages. It uses tags to structure content.

exercises.question: What is an HTML tag?
exercises.answer: A keyword wrapped in angle brackets that tells the browser how to display content
exercises.explain:
Tags like

,

, and
tell the browser what type of content they contain.
choices: A keyword wrapped in angle brackets that tells the browser how to display content

exercises.question: What is an HTML element?
exercises.answer: A tag, its attributes, and the content inside it
exercises.explain:
An element is complete: the opening tag, everything inside, and the closing tag. Example:

Hello

is one element.
choices: A tag, its attributes, and the content inside it

exercises.question: What is an HTML attribute?
exercises.answer: Extra information added to a tag that modifies its behavior or appearance
exercises.explain: Attributes like class, id, href, and src provide additional details. They go inside the opening tag.
choices: Extra information added to a tag that modifies its behavior or appearance

exercises.question: What does the browser do with HTML?
exercises.answer: Reads tags and renders them as formatted web page content on screen
exercises.explain: Browsers interpret HTML tags and display them as text, images, links, and other visual elements.
choices: Reads tags and renders them as formatted web page content on screen

exercises.question: What is the basic HTML page structure?
exercises.answer: <!DOCTYPE html>, <html>, <head>, <body>, and closing tags
exercises.explain: Every HTML page starts with DOCTYPE to declare the type, then html root. The head contains metadata; the body contains visible content.

exercises.question: What goes inside the <head> tag?
exercises.answer: Metadata like title, description, links to CSS, and character encoding
exercises.explain: The head contains information about the page (not visible content): title, viewport, stylesheets, scripts.
choices: Metadata like title, description, links to CSS, and character encoding

exercises.question: What goes inside the <body> tag?
exercises.answer: All visible page content like text, images, links, and buttons
exercises.explain: Everything users see on the page goes in the body: headings, paragraphs, images, forms, etc.
choices: All visible page content like text, images, links, and buttons

exercises.question: What does the <title> tag do?
exercises.answer: Sets the page name shown in the browser tab and search results
exercises.explain: The title appears in the browser tab and helps search engines understand the page.
choices: Creates a heading on the page
Sets the page name shown in the browser tab and search results

exercises.question: What does the <meta> tag do?
exercises.answer: Provides metadata about the page like character encoding and viewport settings
exercises.explain: Meta tags give the browser instructions. The charset meta declares UTF-8 encoding; viewport tells mobile how to display the page.
choices: Provides metadata about the page like character encoding and viewport settings

units.title: Text and Links
units.tip: HTML provides tags for different types of text: headings for titles, paragraphs for body text, and lists for grouped items. Links connect pages. Images embed pictures.

exercises.question: What are heading tags used for?
exercises.answer: Creating titles and subtitles that structure page content hierarchically
exercises.explain: Heading tags <h1> through <h6> organize content. <h1> is the most important and by default the largest; <h6> is the least important and smallest.
choices: Creating titles and subtitles that structure page content hierarchically

exercises.question: What is the difference between <h1> and <h6>?
exercises.answer: <h1> is the most important heading; <h6> is the least important
exercises.explain: h1 is the top level and h6 the lowest, and by default h1 is shown largest. Use h1 for the main page title, h2 for sections, and so on.
choices: They are used for different pages
<h1> is the most important heading; <h6> is the least important

exercises.question:
What is the

tag?
exercises.answer: A paragraph tag that wraps body text
exercises.explain: Paragraphs are the standard way to format text content. The browser adds space before and after each paragraph.
choices: A paragraph tag that wraps body text

exercises.question: What is an unordered list?
exercises.answer: A list with bullet points, created with <ul> and <li> tags
exercises.explain: Unordered lists display items with bullets. Ordered lists use <ol> and show numbers instead.
choices: A list with bullet points, created with <ul> and <li> tags

exercises.question: What does the <li> tag represent?
exercises.answer: A single item in a list
exercises.explain: <li> stands for list item. Every item in a <ul> or <ol> must be wrapped in <li>.
choices: A single item in a list

exercises.question: What is the <a> tag?
exercises.answer: A link tag that connects to other pages or resources
exercises.explain: <a> creates clickable links. The href attribute specifies where the link goes.
choices: A link tag that connects to other pages or resources

exercises.question: What does the href attribute do?
exercises.answer: Specifies the destination URL or page the link points to
exercises.explain: href stands for Hypertext Reference. Example: Click here links to page.html.
choices: Specifies the destination URL or page the link points to

exercises.question: What is the tag?
exercises.answer: A tag that embeds an image in the page
exercises.explain: displays pictures. It is a void element, so it has no closing tag. The src attribute specifies the image file.
choices: A tag that embeds an image in the page

exercises.question: What does the alt attribute in do?
exercises.answer: Provides descriptive text when the image cannot be displayed
exercises.explain: Alt text appears if the image fails to load and helps screen readers describe the image for accessibility.
choices: Provides descriptive text when the image cannot be displayed

exercises.question: How do you create an internal link to another page in your website?
exercises.answer: Link text
exercises.explain: Use a relative path (page.html) for pages in your site or a full URL for external links.

units.title: Semantic HTML and Forms
units.tip: Semantic tags like <header>, <nav>, <main>, and <footer> describe the meaning of content, not just how it looks. Forms collect user input via text fields, buttons, and checkboxes.

exercises.question: What is semantic HTML?
exercises.answer: Using tags that describe the meaning of content, not just its appearance
exercises.explain: Semantic tags like <article>, <section>, and <header> tell search engines and accessibility tools what content means.
choices: Using tags that describe the meaning of content, not just its appearance

exercises.question: What does the <header> tag represent?
exercises.answer: The introductory part of a page or section, usually with title and navigation
exercises.explain: Headers typically contain a logo, title, and navigation links. There can be multiple headers in a page.
choices: The top of the browser window
The introductory part of a page or section, usually with title and navigation

exercises.question: What does the <nav> tag do?
exercises.answer: Wraps navigation links and menus
exercises.explain: <nav> marks navigation areas. Screen readers and search engines understand it as a navigation section.

exercises.question: What does the <main> tag represent?
exercises.answer: The primary content area of the page
exercises.explain: <main> contains the unique content specific to this page. Use it once per page.
choices: The primary content area of the page

exercises.question: What does the <footer> tag contain?
exercises.answer: Secondary information like copyright, links, and contact details
exercises.explain: Footers usually sit at the bottom of a page or section and hold secondary information such as copyright, related links and contact details.
choices: Secondary information like copyright, links, and contact details

exercises.question: What is the <form> tag?
exercises.answer: A container for input elements that collects user data
exercises.explain: Forms let users enter information. They can be submitted to a server for processing.
choices: A container for input elements that collects user data

exercises.question: What does the <input> tag do?
exercises.answer: Creates a field where users can enter data
exercises.explain: <input> creates text fields, checkboxes, radio buttons, and more. The type attribute determines the input kind.
choices: Creates a field where users can enter data

exercises.question: What does the type="email" attribute do?
exercises.answer: Creates an input field that validates email format
exercises.explain: Email inputs check that the user enters a valid email address before submission.
choices: Creates an input field that validates email format

exercises.question: What is the <label> tag used for?
exercises.answer: Associates text with input fields for accessibility and clarity
exercises.explain: Labels describe what each input is for. Screen readers read them. Use the for attribute to connect label to input.
choices: Associates text with input fields for accessibility and clarity

exercises.question: What does the <button> tag do?
exercises.answer: Creates a clickable button, usually to submit a form or trigger an action
exercises.explain: Buttons can submit forms or run JavaScript code when clicked.
choices: Creates a clickable button, usually to submit a form or trigger an action

units.title: CSS Fundamentals
units.tip: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls how HTML looks. Selectors choose elements. Properties describe what to change. Values are what to change it to. Specificity determines which rule wins when conflicts occur.

exercises.question: What does CSS stand for?
exercises.answer: Cascading Style Sheets
exercises.explain: CSS is used to style HTML elements. Cascading means rules can override each other based on specificity.

exercises.question: What is a CSS selector?
exercises.answer: A pattern that targets HTML elements to apply styles to them
exercises.explain: Selectors like p, .class, and #id choose which elements receive the styles inside the rule.
choices: A pattern that targets HTML elements to apply styles to them

exercises.question: What is a CSS property?
exercises.answer: The aspect of an element you want to change, like color or size
exercises.explain: Properties like color, background, margin, and font-size specify what attribute to modify.
choices: The aspect of an element you want to change, like color or size

exercises.question: What is the syntax of a basic CSS rule?
exercises.answer: selector { property: value; }
exercises.explain: A rule has a selector, then curly braces with property-value pairs separated by colons and semicolons.

exercises.question: What is the difference between a class selector and an ID selector?
exercises.answer: Classes start with . and can be reused; IDs start with # and are unique to one element
exercises.explain: Use classes for multiple elements; use IDs for single unique elements. Example: .button vs #header
choices: Classes start with . and can be reused; IDs start with # and are unique to one element

exercises.question: What does Cascading mean in CSS?
exercises.answer: Rules lower in the stylesheet override earlier rules when they conflict
exercises.explain: If two rules apply to the same element, the one written later wins (unless overridden by specificity).
choices: Rules lower in the stylesheet override earlier rules when they conflict

exercises.question: What is CSS specificity?
exercises.answer: A ranking system that determines which rule applies when multiple selectors target the same element
exercises.explain: ID selectors are most specific, then classes, then element selectors. Higher specificity wins.
choices: A ranking system that determines which rule applies when multiple selectors target the same element

exercises.question: Which has higher specificity: an element selector or a class selector?
exercises.answer: A class selector
exercises.explain: Class selectors (.class) beat element selectors (p). ID selectors (#id) beat both.

exercises.question: What does !important do in CSS?
exercises.answer: Forces a rule to apply, overriding other specificity rules
exercises.explain: !important makes a rule high priority. Use it sparingly as it can make debugging harder.
choices: Forces a rule to apply, overriding other specificity rules

exercises.question: What is inheritance in CSS?
exercises.answer: Child elements automatically inherit certain properties from their parents
exercises.explain: Properties like color and font-size pass down to child elements. Some properties like margin do not inherit.
choices: Child elements automatically inherit certain properties from their parents

units.title: The Box Model and Layout
units.tip: Every HTML element is a box. The box model includes margin, border, padding, and content. Display controls how elements behave. Flexbox and Grid are modern layout tools.

exercises.question: What is the CSS box model?
exercises.answer: The structure of every element: content, padding, border, and margin
exercises.explain: From inside to outside: content (text/images), padding (inside space), border (edge), margin (outside space).
choices: The structure of every element: content, padding, border, and margin

exercises.question: What does padding do?
exercises.answer: Adds space inside the element, between the content and the border
exercises.explain: Padding is inside the box. It pushes the content away from the edges.
choices: Adds space inside the element, between the content and the border

exercises.question: What does margin do?
exercises.answer: Adds space outside the element, between it and other elements
exercises.explain: Margin is outside the box. It creates distance between elements.
choices: Adds space outside the element, between it and other elements

exercises.question: What is the border?
exercises.answer: A line drawn around the padding and content
exercises.explain: Borders can have style (solid, dashed), color, and thickness.
choices: A line drawn around the padding and content

exercises.question: How do you set equal padding on all four sides?
exercises.answer: padding: 10px;
exercises.explain: One value sets all four sides equal. (Four values also work, in the order top, right, bottom, left, but one value is the shortest way.)

exercises.question: What does the display property control?
exercises.answer: How an element behaves: inline, block, or other layout modes
exercises.explain: display changes whether elements stack vertically (block), sit side-by-side (inline), or use flexbox/grid.
choices: How an element behaves: inline, block, or other layout modes
The stacking order of overlapping elements

exercises.question: What is a block element?
exercises.answer: An element that takes up the full width and starts on a new line
exercises.explain:
Block elements like
,

, and

stack vertically. Width and margin apply.
choices: An element on the same line as others
An element that takes up the full width and starts on a new line

exercises.question: What is an inline element?
exercises.answer: An element that sits on the same line as other content and only takes up needed width
exercises.explain: Inline elements like <span> and <a> flow with text. Width and height do not apply.
choices: An element that is always centered
An element that always takes up full width
An element that sits on the same line as other content and only takes up needed width

exercises.question: What is Flexbox?
exercises.answer: A layout mode that arranges elements in rows or columns with flexible sizing
exercises.explain: Flexbox makes it easy to create responsive layouts. Use display: flex on the parent container.
choices: A layout mode that arranges elements in rows or columns with flexible sizing

exercises.question: What is CSS Grid?
exercises.answer: A layout system that arranges elements in rows and columns using a grid template
exercises.explain: Grid is powerful for complex layouts. Use display: grid on the parent container.
choices: A layout system that arranges elements in rows and columns using a grid template

units.title: Responsive and Accessible Design
units.tip: Responsive design adapts to different screen sizes using media queries and relative units. Accessibility ensures all users can navigate and understand your site, including those with disabilities.

exercises.question: What is responsive web design?
exercises.answer: Designing pages that adapt and look good on all screen sizes
exercises.explain: Responsive layouts adjust for phones, tablets, and desktops. Users get a good experience everywhere.
choices: Designing pages that adapt and look good on all screen sizes
Using one fixed width for all devices

exercises.question: What is a media query?
exercises.answer: CSS rules that apply only when certain conditions are met, like screen width
exercises.explain: Media queries let you change styles based on device width, orientation, or other features.
choices: CSS rules that apply only when certain conditions are met, like screen width

exercises.question: How do you write a media query for screens 768px wide or narrower?
exercises.answer: @media (max-width: 768px) { }
exercises.explain: This rule applies styles only to devices with screens 768px wide or smaller.

exercises.question: What is the viewport meta tag?
exercises.answer: A meta tag that tells mobile browsers how to scale and display your page
exercises.explain: Without it, many mobile browsers lay the page out at a wide desktop width and shrink it down. The tag makes the page match the device width: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
choices: A meta tag that tells mobile browsers how to scale and display your page

exercises.question: What is a relative unit in CSS?
exercises.answer: A size that is relative to another value, like the parent element or viewport
exercises.explain: Relative units (em, rem, %, vw) adapt to context. Absolute units (px, pt) do not scale.
choices: A size that is relative to another value, like the parent element or viewport

exercises.question: What is web accessibility?
exercises.answer: Designing websites so everyone can use them, including people with disabilities
exercises.explain: Accessibility helps users with vision, hearing, mobility, and cognitive disabilities navigate your site.
choices: Designing websites so everyone can use them, including people with disabilities

exercises.question: What is the alt attribute used for in images?
exercises.answer: Describing the image for users who cannot see it and for search engines
exercises.explain: Screen readers read alt text. Good alt text describes what the image shows.
choices: Describing the image for users who cannot see it and for search engines

exercises.question: What is a screen reader?
exercises.answer: Software that reads page content aloud for users with vision disabilities
exercises.explain: Screen readers navigate HTML. Good semantic HTML and alt text help them work correctly.
choices: Software that reads page content aloud for users with vision disabilities

exercises.question: What is color contrast?
exercises.answer: The difference in brightness between text and background colors
exercises.explain: Good contrast (dark text on light background) helps users with low vision read your site.
choices: The difference in brightness between text and background colors

exercises.question: Why is semantic HTML important for accessibility?
exercises.answer: It tells screen readers and assistive technology the meaning of content
exercises.explain: Semantic tags like <nav>, <button>, and <label> help accessibility tools understand your page.
choices: It tells screen readers and assistive technology the meaning of content
